ancient.name: Sima de los Huesos
ancient.story_individual:
Around 400,000 years ago, a hominin died and their remains ended up in what would become known as Sima de los Huesos (Pit of Bones) in northern Spain. The individual's remains, including a femur which would later yield crucial DNA evidence, were preserved alongside approximately 28 other individuals in the cave system at Atapuerca. While researchers cannot determine this individual's biological sex, they know they belonged to a population that showed Neanderthal-like features in their skeletal morphology.

The remarkable preservation of their DNA was made possible by the stable, cold conditions within the cave. When the femur was analyzed in 2014, the DNA retrieved from it represented the oldest human DNA ever sequenced, pushing back the boundaries of ancient DNA research by hundreds of thousands of years. The mitochondrial DNA unexpectedly showed closer affinity to Denisovans than to Neanderthals, despite the skeletal characteristics of the population.

The recovery of such ancient DNA was a major technical achievement that required innovative methods to deal with highly degraded genetic material. While we don't know the details of this individual's life - what they ate, how they lived, or how they died - their genetic legacy has provided crucial insights into human evolution and the complex relationships between ancient hominin populations.

Subsequent nuclear DNA analysis of Sima de los Huesos hominins revealed a closer connection to Neanderthals than the mtDNA initially suggested, adding another fascinating layer to this individual's story.

References

  • Meyer, M., Fu, Q., Aximu-Petri, A. et al. A mitochondrial genome sequence of a hominin from Sima de los Huesos. Nature 505, 403–406 (2014). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12788

  • Meyer, M., Arsuaga, JL., de Filippo, C. et al. Nuclear DNA sequences from the Middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos hominins. Nature 531, 504–507 (2016). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature17405

Pictured: Cranium 17 of the Sima de los Huesos, from an individual from the same location and time period. Nohemi Sala, Juan Luis Arsuaga, Ana Pantoja-Pérez, Adrián Pablos, Ignacio Martínez, Rolf M. famous.name: Richard III of England
famous.story_individual:
Richard III was King of England and Lord of Ireland for only two years from 1483 until he died in 1485.

He came to the throne under a cloud of suspicion. His brother’s minor son, Edward, was preparing to be crowned king when Edward’s brother’s marriage was posthumously declared bigamous and his offspring through that marriage were no longer eligible to ascend the throne.

His two sons became the infamous “Princes in the Tower,” imprisoned in the Tower of London and never seen again. It was rumored that Richard ordered their murders.

Richard isn’t most famous for what occurred during his life, but due to the circumstances surrounding his death, burial, and subsequent exhumation.

Richard died in battle near Leicestershire and was buried unceremoniously, apparently in the Grey Friars Priory.

Portrait of Richard III of England, painted c.1520

In 2012, a skeleton was excavated in a car park where the Grey Friars Abbey was previously located. Turi King, from the University of Leicester, DNA tested the remains and concluded that the evidence for the remains being those of Richard III was overwhelming, thereby solving the mystery of where Richard was actually buried and what happened to his remains.

Richard’s mtDNA haplogroup was J1c2c3 and a perfect match with present-day matrilineal relatives. His Y-DNA haplogroup was however inconsistent with present-day patrilineal relatives and shows that there is at least one false-paternity event in the family tree of either Richard III or the present-day DNA-tested relatives.

Richard III was the last king of the House of York and the last of the Plantagenet dynasty.

References

  • King, T. E., Fortes, G. G., Balaresque, P., Thomas, M. G., Balding, D., Delser, P. M., Neumann, R., Parson, W., Knapp, M., Walsh, S., Tonasso, L., Holt, J., Kayser, M., Appleby, J., Forster, P., Ekserdjian, D., Hofreiter, M., & Schürer, K. (2014). Identification of the remains of King Richard III. Nature Communications, 5(1), 1-8. https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms6631

Biographical information sourced from Wikipedia and WikiTree.

famous.name: Ilse von dem Berge
famous.story_individual:
Ilse von dem Berge (c. 1557 – after 6 June 1624) was a noblewoman born in Gümse, Lüneburg, in what is now Lower Saxony, Germany.

Ilse's mother was Katharine von der Schulenburg (1542–1582), a member of the influential von der Schulenburg family. Through Katharine, Ilse traced her direct maternal ancestry to the noble families of von Quitzow, von Arnim, von Bredow, and von Platen, reflecting strong dynastic ties within the German high nobility.

The known maternal line is:

  • Ursula von Platen (~1430– ) married Hans von Bredow

  • Anna von Bredow (~1450–after 1515) married Henning III von Arnim (1445–1501)

  • Margareta von Arnim (1487–after 1542) married George II (Jürgen) von Quitzow (1460–1527)

  • Ilse (Catharina) von Quitzow (1518–1591) married Levin I von der Schulenburg (1510–1569)

  • Katharine von der Schulenburg (1542–1582) married Vicke von dem Berge (- 1566)

  • Ilse von dem Berge (c. 1557–after 1624) married Dietrich III von Maltzahn (1552 -1599).

The male line of the von dem Berge family ended with the death of Fritz von dem Berge in 1623. Descendants of the Maltzahn family inherited his estates through his sister, Ilse von dem Berge, who had married Dietrich III von Maltzahn.

Ilse von dem Berge has been confirmed as the most recent common maternal ancestor for three mtFull tested individuals at FamilyTreeDNA. All share the mitochondrial DNA haplogroup J1c2b, supporting the documented genealogical lines. Given the noble status and extensive marriage connections of these families, Ursula von Platen’s mitochondrial lineage was likely well-represented among the German nobility.

Additional information about the shared mtDNA lineage (J1c2b) can be found at Anbytarforum. Historical information sourced from Geni.com, Wikipedia and Baltische Studien Vol. 5–6, p. 109. This biography was compiled with assistance from an AI model. Image: Coat of arms for the von dem Berge family by Magnus Bjuhr (CC0).

famous.name: Dolley Madison
famous.story_individual:
Dolley Madison (née Payne) was the wife of U.S. President James Madison and is regarded as one of America's most influential First Ladies, serving in this role from 1809 to 1817. Before marrying Madison, she was briefly married to John Todd, who died along with her youngest son in the 1793 yellow fever epidemic in Philadelphia.

As First Lady, Dolley Madison was known for her gracious manners and social skills, which helped establish the role of the President's wife as public hostess and set standards for future First Ladies. She is particularly remembered for her actions during the British invasion of Washington in 1814, when she helped save important national treasures, including the famous portrait of George Washington, from the burning White House.

Before her time as First Lady, she assisted Thomas Jefferson, who was a widower, with hostess duties at the White House during his presidency. She was known for her ability to navigate complex political situations through social gatherings, helping to bridge partisan divides in the early republic. Her weekly "drawing room" events became a Washington institution, mixing politicians from different parties with international diplomats and local society.

After James Madison's death in 1836, Dolley faced financial difficulties but remained a respected figure in Washington society. She lived in the capital until her death in 1849. In 2025, DNA analysis of her sister Lucy Payne's burial at Harewood Cemetery provided new insights into the Madison family's maternal lineage, allowing researchers to determine the mitochondrial DNA signature shared by both sisters.

famous.name: Lucy Payne Washington Todd
famous.story_individual:
Lucinda (Lucy) Payne was an American woman who had significant connections to prominent 19th century political families. She was the sister of Dolley Madison (wife of U.S. President James Madison) and married twice - first to George Steptoe Washington, a nephew of President George Washington, and later to Supreme Court Justice Thomas Todd.

Her burial at Harewood Cemetery was conclusively identified through a groundbreaking 2025 DNA study. The study analyzed remains from three unmarked graves excavated in 1999 and definitively identified Payne and her two sons - George Steptoe Washington Jr. and Dr. Samuel Walter Washington. Through advanced DNA analysis techniques, researchers confirmed her maternal relationship to both sons and connected her to living Washington descendants, particularly Samuel Walter Washington, who was confirmed as her great-great-great-grandson.

Lucy Payne was buried at Harewood Cemetery alongside her two sons, with her remains identified as "Burial 4" during the excavation. The scientific confirmation of her burial location and maternal relationships has allowed for proper marking of her grave and those of her children, preserving her place in both Washington family history and early American heritage.

famous.name: Johan Glans
famous.story_individual:
Johan Magnus Glans, born in Eslöv, Sweden, is a prominent Swedish stand-up comedian and actor known for his sharp wit and versatile performances. He entered the comedy scene in 1994, gaining early fame through collaborations with comedian David Batra on Swedish TV shows, and debuted on television in 1995. Highlights of his career include starring in popular series like Swedish Dicks (2016-present) as Axel, serving as a team leader on SVT's Tror du jag ljuger? since 2016, and recent projects such as the 2020 SVT Christmas calendar Mirakel and the 2021 Netflix series Home Invasion. His film work features the stand-up special Johan Glans: World Tour of Skåne (2008). Glans was awarded the Pirate Prize in 2018 for his comedic contributions.

On the family front, his father, Tom Glans (born 1947), discovered at age 71 through a DNA test—while researching family history—that his own father (Johan's paternal grandfather) was not his biological parent. Tom initially found the revelation shocking, but later embraced it as a positive chapter in his life, even sharing the story in a public lecture. Johan’s detailed Y-DNA haplogroup was determined through Big Y testing of his father, and his detailed mtDNA haplogroup was determined through mtFull Sequence testing of his mother, Britt-Marie Glans.

Biography in part generated using xAI (2025) Grok (Version 3) [Large language model].

famous.name: Vinia Tsopelas
famous.story_individual:
The distinguished Greek pianist Vinia Tsopelas was born in Athens, with maternal origins from Sfakia on the island of Crete. After graduating from the Athens Conservatory with the highest distinction, she continued her studies in Paris with Yvonne Lefèbure and Nadia Boulanger, and at Juilliard in New York under Ilona Kabos, Adele Marcus, Guido Agosti, and Nadia Reisenberg, graduating with honors. She also studied for many years with Gina Bachauer, being her closest protégée.

In 1979, Tsopelas won the Gina Bachauer International Competition in Dallas, Texas, launching an international career. She has performed with major orchestras, including Philadelphia, Saint Louis, Dallas, Sacramento, Phoenix, and Santa Barbara, and at renowned venues such as Alice Tully Hall at the Lincoln Center, the Ambassador Auditorium in Los Angeles, the Legion of Honor Museum in San Francisco, and the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC. She has also performed in Belgium, Denmark, England, Germany, Israel, Spain, Thailand, and in Greece, where she inaugurated Megaron the Athens Concert Hall with her performance.

As the first Professor of Piano Performance in Greece at the University of Macedonia, Thessaloniki, she led masterclasses and student exchange programs worldwide. Frequently serving as a juror for international competitions, she has also represented Greece as a cultural ambassador, performing for presidents, royals, dignitaries and audiences worldwide. She has also premiered works by contemporary Greek composers, notably Manos Hadjidakis.

famous.name: Clara Ward
famous.story_individual:
Clara Ward was born into extraordinary privilege as the youngest daughter of Captain Eber Ward, Detroit's first millionaire. Her father's immense wealth and her striking beauty would shape the course of her unconventional life.

After proving resistant to traditional schooling, Clara was steered toward what seemed the only appropriate path for a wealthy young woman of her era - an advantageous marriage. At just 17 years old, she married Prince Joseph de Caraman-Chimay of Belgium in 1890, becoming the Princesse de Caraman-Chimay. The marriage produced two children, but by 1896, the relationship had become strained and the young family relocated to Paris.

It was in Paris where Clara, then 23, truly began to make her mark on society, quickly earning a reputation as "the most riotous" American in the capital. Her life took its most dramatic turn during a fateful evening at the exclusive Café Gaillard, where she encountered Rigó Jancsi, a Hungarian Romani violinist playing from table to table. The attraction was immediate - within just ten days, the Princess and the "Gypsy fiddler" had run away together to Budapest, creating an international scandal that captivated the press.

She would marry again after Rigó, and ultimately died from pneumonia at her villa in Padua, Italy, while living with her third husband. Throughout her life, she remained a figure of fascination, with countless stories - both true and embellished - circulating about her various adventures and misadventures. Her legacy stands as that of a fearless rebel who used her beauty and wealth to chart her own course through the rigid social structures of the Gilded Age.

Her mtDNA haplogroup was determined by mtFull testing of her matrilineal relative and documented on WikiTree.

famous.name: Tony Lupien
famous.story_individual:
Ulysses John "Tony" Lupien Jr. was a well-rounded athlete and scholar who made his mark in both academics and professional baseball. Born in Chelmsford, Massachusetts, Lupien attended Harvard University, where he captained both the baseball team (as a junior) and basketball team (as a senior), and played quarterback for the freshman football team, graduating in 1939.

Making his Major League Baseball debut in 1940 with the Boston Red Sox, Lupien went on to play first base for three MLB teams including the Philadelphia Phillies and Chicago White Sox. A left-handed batter, he compiled solid career statistics over 614 games, finishing with a .268 batting average, 18 home runs, 230 RBI, and 285 runs scored. His extra-base hits included 92 doubles and 30 triples, while he also demonstrated speed on the basepaths with 57 stolen bases.

After his playing career, Lupien transitioned to coaching baseball at Dartmouth College, where he served until his retirement in 1977. His legacy in sports continued through his family - he was the grandfather of professional wrestler and Hollywood actor John Cena.

His mtDNA haplogroup was determined by mtFull testing of his matrilineal relative and documented on WikiTree.

Biographical information sourced from Wikipedia. Biography in part generated using Anthropic (2025) Claude 3.5 Sonnet [Large language model]. Pictured: Tony Lupien from 1949 Bowman baseball card, Bowman Gum, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Neanderthal Man
famous.story_individual:
Neanderthals were first named and unearthed in 1856 in the Neander Valley of Germany, three full years before Darwin published his book On the Origin of Species. In his writings, Darwin only briefly wrote about human evolution and did not mention anything about the newly named Neanderthals. Coincidentally, by 1848, a Neanderthal skeleton had already been discovered in Gibraltar. That specimen, however, had remained uncharacterized in science. So, as fate would have it, the German team is credited with discovering the new species, and the name Neanderthal still remains. Neanderthal Man (seen pictured as a reconstruction) from Feldhofer cave in Neander Valley lived approximately 40,000 years ago.

Today, we know much more about these cousins of Homo sapiens (humans), when and where they lived and how they may have mated with our stone-age ancestors. In 2008, a team led by Nobel Laureate Svante Pääbo sequenced the first Neanderthal genome, and just months after that publication, anthropologists discovered that Neanderthal DNA still resided in most humans alive today. Yes, humans and Neanderthals had mated.

Although the common evolutionary ancestor to Homo sapiens and Neanderthals lived more than half-a-million years ago, we now know that the Y chromosome of the male Neanderthals sequenced to date came from an introduction event (a mating) between a male archaic human and a female Neanderthal between 370,000 and 100,000 years ago. This, and other new findings, suggests that mixing between human ancestors and Neanderthals occurred early and possibly frequently while they co-existed for millennia in Europe and Asia, which was until approximately 35,000 years ago when Neanderthals went extinct. 

We are fortunate to be living in an amazing time where every year new discoveries add exciting information about humans, our ancestors, and our shared prehistory. The last decade alone has completely reshaped our knowledge and relationship with the once mighty Neanderthals.

Homo neanderthalensis reconstruction - Mr. N

©Neanderthal Museum

The divergence time between modern human and Neanderthal Y chromosomes was estimated by Petr et al. 2020. The evolutionary history of Neanderthal and Denisovan Y chromosomes. The A000-T haplogroup name comes from the ISOGG Y-DNA Haplogroup Tree 2019-2020.
